summary: Describes known open problems in Internet congestion control, including new challenges as networks grow and long-standing issues. They are considered research topics. It is an informational IRTF document.

eli5.summary: Sharing the internet fairly without jamming it is hard. This lists questions that researchers have not yet fully answered.

questions: open research issues in congestion control
why is tcp slow on high-speed networks
subtitle: Open research challenges in keeping the Internet running fairly when capacity is limited.

tldr.problem: Van Jacobson's TCP congestion control algorithms, developed in 1988, struggle with modern high-speed links, heterogeneous networks, and emerging applications. Fundamental tensions exist between stability, fairness, and efficiency.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies seven major open challenges: network support for congestion control, corruption loss recovery, packet size issues, flow startup optimization, multi-domain signaling, traffic precedence, and preventing misbehaving senders. It also discusses underlying issues like stability theory and fairness models.
tldr.outcome: Published as an IRTF consensus document in 2011, it provides a research roadmap for congestion control. The problems remain largely unsolved, with ongoing work in areas like ECN deployment, multipath TCP, and low-priority traffic protocols.

today: RFC 6077 is an informational IRTF document published in February 2011 that maps unsolved research challenges in Internet congestion control. Most of these challenges remain open. ECN deployment has increased but remains incomplete; misbehavior by unresponsive applications continues to grow; multipath TCP development continues; and fundamental questions about fairness metrics and network-assisted approaches remain debated.

sections.title: Background and Foundational Concepts
sections.content:
Congestion control is a distributed algorithm that shares network resources among competing traffic sources. Two components work together: primal congestion control is performed by traffic sources (hosts) that adjust their sending rates based on feedback, and dual congestion control is performed by routers that gather traffic information and signal congestion back to sources. TCP implements primal control; router mechanisms like Random Early Detection (RED) implement dual control.

Van Jacobson's algorithms from 1988 introduced Additive Increase Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD), which has proven highly successful for nearly two decades. However, they assume relatively static network conditions with small bandwidth-delay products (a few dozen packets). Modern networks violate these assumptions: satellite links have extreme latency (seconds), optical networks have massive bandwidth-delay products (millions of packets), wireless links change dynamically, and applications range from interactive voice to bulk file transfer. Additionally, more sophisticated protocols have departed from pure end-to-end design; router-based mechanisms like ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) pass congestion information directly to hosts rather than relying on packet loss alone.
sections.eli5: The basic idea: senders slow down when they lose packets (feeling the congestion), and routers might help by sending early warning messages. But the 1988 design assumes predictable networks, and today's networks are crazy complicated.

sections.title: Heterogeneity, Stability, and Fairness Challenges
sections.content:
Modern congestion control must handle heterogeneity in link capacities (from kilobits per second on radio links to gigabits per second on optical fiber) and path characteristics (latency ranges from microseconds to seconds). Beyond just variation, these characteristics change dynamically due to cross-traffic, routing changes, link-layer mechanisms, and mobility. Congestion control algorithms must react efficiently and stably to this variety without requiring extensive tuning for each scenario.

Stability means the system converges to equilibrium and does not oscillate wildly. Control theory provides mathematical tools, but applying them to realistic networks is difficult. TCP's stability relies on two key aspects: AIMD behavior and the conservation of packets principle (only send when an acknowledgment arrives). Modern approaches question whether the target rate must be inversely proportional to RTT (round-trip time) or only the rate of increase needs to be.

Fairness is deeply contested. The traditional view is that flows sharing a bottleneck should get equal rates (flow-rate fairness). A competing view based on cost economics argues that fairness should be based on congestion-volume: each user should pay a price proportional to the congestion they cause. These lead to fundamentally different protocol designs and are difficult to reconcile.
sections.eli5: Three big questions: (1) can one algorithm work on all types of networks, (2) does it reach a stable state or oscillate, and (3) what is fair—equal rates or equal cost?

sections.title: Network Support and Explicit Signaling
sections.content:
The most critical challenge is balancing functions between endpoints and the network. Implicit mechanisms like RED queue management improve performance without requiring new protocols, but finding optimal parameters is non-trivial. Explicit mechanisms like ECN (one bit) or XCP (per-datagram rate feedback) provide more information but require router implementation and careful design to avoid instability.

XCP (eXplicit Control Protocol) was developed to overcome TCP's inefficiency on high bandwidth-delay product networks. It achieves high utilization with small queue sizes and near-zero drops by decoupling resource utilization from fairness control. However, XCP has limitations: it is locally stable but globally unstable when maximum RTT is much larger than mean RTT, and it can discriminate against heterogeneous traffic. RCP (Rate Control Protocol) focuses on reducing flow completion times instead. Quick-Start is an in-band signaling approach; CADPC/PTP is out-of-band.

A fundamental tension exists with the end-to-end principle: congestion is inherent to networks and requires cooperation between endpoints and routers, yet placing functions in routers increases their complexity and reduces evolvability. Router ALGs (Application Layer Gateways) and middleboxes complicate matters further by splitting end-to-end connections, disrupting congestion control.
sections.eli5: Should routers help by telling hosts how fast to go, or should hosts figure it out themselves? More router help means better performance but less evolvability and more complexity.

sections.title: Multi-Domain and Misbehavior Challenges
sections.content:
In multi-domain networks, the Internet is divided into autonomous systems with different policies and trust boundaries. ECN, which is effective within a domain, faces attacks at domain boundaries: non-compliant networks may erase ECN marks (non-compliance) or create false marks (subversion), causing upstream networks to respond excessively. Two solutions exist: ECN-nonce and re-ECN, but neither is fully robust. Fragmentation complicates ECN-nonce protection, and neither protects against subversion of non-ECN traffic.

Misbehaving senders and receivers pose another challenge. It is not in a receiver's interest to honestly report congestion if it means slower download speeds. It is not in a sender's interest to reduce rate if others will do so instead. Some applications use UDP without congestion control or worse, add more error correction when experiencing loss. Numerous strategies for misbehavior exist, and while most are not yet common, the Internet may increasingly depend on enforcement rather than voluntary compliance.

Pseudowires carrying inelastic traffic (like TDM or ATM) over IP networks illustrate multi-domain complexity: if the PW source rate-limits aggregate traffic, transit providers cannot detect that it is inelastic and may allow it to consume all available bandwidth while responsive TCP flows reduce their rates to zero. This requires mechanisms to enforce fair, robust congestion control without mandating specific algorithms that would harm evolvability.
sections.eli5: In multi-domain networks, networks may cheat on congestion signals, and senders/receivers may cheat to get more bandwidth. How do you prevent cheating without breaking privacy and evolution?

sections.title: Flow Startup, Devices, and Multipath Control
sections.content:
Flow startup is suboptimal in TCP. Slow-start is aggressive early in a flow but then becomes very conservative. For short-lived flows (common in HTTP), the connection may never leave slow-start. The impact on overall network stability is unclear. Questions remain about optimal initial congestion window sizes and how to start aggressively without causing collapse.

RTT estimation is critical for many congestion control schemes, but optimal measurement frequency, filter design, and handling of missing feedback are not well understood. Congestion control depends on knowing round-trip time, yet measuring it accurately in heterogeneous networks with varying delay is difficult. Default values are typically conservative and may not be optimal.

Malfunctioning devices have historically hindered deployment of beneficial features. ECN deployment was delayed by broken firewalls; Window Scaling was disabled in many implementations due to middlebox bugs. Standards should define behavior for all field values to ensure forward compatibility.

Multipath congestion control offers benefits in resilience and resource efficiency. MPTCP (Multipath TCP) allows endpoints to pool resources across multiple paths, improving robustness. However, interactions with traffic engineering and whether multipath control can outperform network-controlled routing remain open research questions. Other challenges include congestion control in multi-layered networks with lower-layer mechanisms, and handling ALGs and transparent proxies that disrupt end-to-end control.
sections.eli5: Other issues: new flows start too fast or too slow, measuring network delay is hard, some routers/firewalls break new features, and using multiple paths at once is promising but still being figured out.
